segments.text: We log in as behemoth one and look at the binary.
ls shows it is setuid to behemoth two, and file says it is a thirty-two bit Intel executable, not stripped.
We disassemble main with objdump: it loads the address of a buffer sixty-seven bytes below the frame pointer and calls gets on it.
gets reads until a newline with no bound, so this is a classic stack overflow: the saved frame pointer sits at offset sixty-seven and the return address at offset seventy-one.
We inspect the protections: readelf shows the stack is marked executable, and address randomisation is off.
That combination means we do not need a return-to-libc chain; we can simply place shellcode on the stack and jump to it.
Then we write the shellcode in vim.
First the header: thirty-two bit mode, the global entry point, and the start label.
It writes a marker so our sweep can detect a successful jump. It pushes a zero and the marker bytes onto the stack, then points at them and calls write.
Then it calls geteuid, setreuid with that id twice,
and setuid with the same id so the privilege survives the exec. It calls geteuid again, moves the id into place, and invokes setuid.

And finally execve on slash bin slash sh. It pushes a zero, then slash slash s h, then slash b i n, points the first argument at the stack, builds the argument list from it, clears the environment pointer, loads eleven as the syscall number, and triggers the interrupt.
We assemble it with nasm, extract the raw bytes with objcopy, and print them with xxd: seventy-eight bytes.
The payload is seventy-one NOP bytes, then the candidate return address, then the shellcode, then a newline.
The exploit forks once per candidate address, feeds the payload on standard input, and watches for the marker.
When it finds the address that lands in the shellcode, it runs the binary again with that address and feeds the shell commands.
We get a shell as behemoth two and read the password, and the level is solved.
